Note · Christensen — The Innovator's Dilemma

4 min read976 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-christensen-innovators-dilemma.md

Canon · Cluster: Landscape & Competitive Awareness · Maps to Course 04 (Competitive Strategy), Course 10 (Entrepreneurship)

  • Source: Clayton Christensen, The Innovator's Dilemma (1997)
  • Core claim: Good companies fail not despite doing everything right, but because of it. Rational, customer-driven decision-making can be the mechanism of your own disruption.
  • Framework:
  • Incumbents listen to their best customers, invest in their most profitable (sustaining) products, and rationally ignore small, low-margin emerging markets.
  • Disruptors enter at the bottom (or create a new market) with a product that's worse on traditional metrics but better on a new dimension the incumbent isn't tracking — convenience, price, simplicity, accessibility.
  • The disruptor improves until it's "good enough" on the traditional metric — and by then it's too late for the incumbent to respond.
  • Sustaining vs. disruptive innovation is the core distinction; incumbents reliably win the former, lose the latter.
  • Applies when: evaluating a cheap/"inferior" new entrant — the question is which dimension it competes on, not whether it's currently worse than you.
  • Breaks when: the theory is over-applied — not every cheap entrant is a disruptor; many are just bad products that stay bad (Christensen famously mis-predicted the iPhone as non-disruptive). It's strong on why incumbents fail, weak as a prediction tool (hard to tell ex-ante which low-end entrant has the improvement trajectory). And the prescription — "set up an autonomous unit" — frequently fails in practice. Pairs with Grove's inflection points (canon grove only the paranoid survive) and Helmer's counter-positioning.

  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-06 — HBR "Disruptive Innovation Explained" transcript, youtube.com/watch?v=qDrMAzCHFUU) Christensen himself supplies the cleanest targeting heuristic, and the book-specific transcript preserves it verbatim: when Andy Grove pressed him on what disruption meant for Intel, Christensen refused to prescribe — "if I'd have been suckered into telling Andy Grove what he should do, I'd have been killed because he knew so much more about microprocessors than I ever would know." He handed over the theory, and Grove worked out the answer himself: "Grove said, oh I get it… they had two companies coming at him from below and Intel needs to go down and not let them go up against us." That's the founder's correct use of the book — a lens you apply to your own market, not a forecast you outsource to the author. The same transcript flags the over-application risk too: Christensen's confidence reads as post-hoc (mini-mills, PCs, smartphones all narrated after the fact), which is exactly why the r/strategy practitioner canon leans on operational trade-off books — Lafley/Martin's "Playing to Win" (102↑) and "Bulletproof Problem Solving" (87↑) — that force ex-ante where-to-play/how-to-win choices Christensen's taxonomy can't.

  • Researched layer (updated 2026-06-06)

  • Canonical explanation (sourced): Christensen's mechanism is the rational trap. A disruptive innovation "generally has to cause you to go after new markets, people who aren't your customers… something that is just so much more affordable and simple that your current customers can't buy it" — so the incumbent's choice becomes "should we make better products that we could sell for better profits to our best customers? Or maybe we ought to make worse products that none of our customers would buy that would ruin our margins" (Clayton Christensen, HBR — "Disruptive Innovation Explained," youtube.com/watch?v=qDrMAzCHFUU). Listening to your best customers is the mechanism of failure, not a deviation from doing things right.
  • Real application (mined): the Oxford lecture works the cases in full detail. Steel mini-mills entered at rebar — "a doggy dog commodity… their gross margins were only 7%" — so "the integrated mills were just relieved to get out of the rebar business" and fled up-market chasing the "12% gross margins" a tier above, exactly as the disruptor wanted: "in pursuit of profit, the giant is motivated to flee rather than fight you." The auto case mirrors it — Toyota came in not with Lexuses but "rusty little subcompacts in the 1960s called Coronas" so cheap that "the rebar of humanity, people we call college students, can own a car," then marched up to Lexus; "Kia and Hyundai have stolen the bottom of the market from Toyota… why would they ever want to defend the lowest profit part of their product line when they have the privilege of competing in luxury cars against Mercedes?" (Saïd Business School, Oxford, youtube.com/watch?v=rpkoCZ4vBSI).
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: the theory is descriptively gorgeous and predictively weak. Every case in the transcript is narrated in hindsight — even Christensen's cleanest win (Intel) works because he refused to predict and handed Grove a lens instead. The r/strategy practitioner canon routes around this gap by privileging trade-off frameworks that force a decision before the outcome is known: "Playing to Win" (102↑) and "Bulletproof Problem Solving" (87↑) top the list, while Innovator's Dilemma itself isn't the thread people reach for — the "explains everything, predicts nothing" worry, made concrete.
  • Sources in corpus: Harvard Business Review — "Disruptive Innovation Explained" (youtube.com/watch?v=qDrMAzCHFUU) · Saïd Business School, Oxford — "Clayton Christensen: Disruptive innovation" (youtube.com/watch?v=rpkoCZ4vBSI) · Startup Grind — "Clayton Christensen on How to Build a Disruptive Business" (youtube.com/watch?v=Zn6-KksdOgE) · r/strategy "Playing to Win: How Strategy Really Works" (102↑), "Bulletproof Problem Solving: The One Skill That Changes Everything" (87↑).
